basis:
WHAT THIS FILE IS. The observed ENVELOPE of every entry the speed gate measures, recorded from four dispatches of one tree on the cell that reads it: ubuntu-latest, image ubuntu24/20260927.320, runner 2.337.0. Runs 36832215161, 36832519319, 36832824918 and 36833056763, between 2026-10-01T07:46Z and 07:56Z, which is the window measured_at records. Each dispatch ran ROUNDS=2 and the two rounds within a dispatch agree to about 2%; n records the four dispatch-level observations the min and max below were taken from. Every figure here was recomputed from those runs' speed-junit-reports artifacts — the raw `time` and `gh-wall` attributes across both rounds of each dispatch, reduced to one per-run minimum per entry — rather than taken from any run summary. No number in this file is invented and each traces to one of those four runs.

PROVENANCE OF measured_commit. 3c30eca is the REMOTE head the four dispatches resolved `--ref issue-81-82` against, not a local checkout, and commits landed after it do not change what was measured: this document records a measurement, and the tree it was taken from is identified by that sha. A reader who finds 3c30eca is not an ancestor of the current head should NOT conclude the file is stale. It was stale once, deliberately, and the fix is recorded below.

WHY AN ENVELOPE AND NOT A NUMBER. CPU seconds exclude steal, so a co-tenant does not reach them — that is what makes them a magnitude where elapsed time is not. They are still hardware-dependent: a faster or narrower core runs the same instructions in fewer CPU seconds, and the ubuntu-latest pool spans instance types. Observed min-to-max across the four dispatches:

    counter::unit-suite            16.593450 - 23.203122   39.8%
    e2e::bench.render               0.056494 -  0.084195   49.0%
    e2e::bench.render-impact        1.018783 -  1.351400   32.6%
    e2e::bench.render-responsiveness 0.060249 -  0.080077   32.9%

The whole vector moves together — a faster run is faster on every entry at once — which is a property of the machine and not of the code. A single stored value plus a budget wide enough to cover that would need a tolerance above 1.0 on some entries, which is not a loose gate but a gate that cannot fire. So an entry stores the range it was observed over, and the head must clear `observed maximum x (1 + tolerance)`.

WHY THE TOLERANCE IS THE OBSERVED SPREAD, AND WHY THAT IS NOT 0.25. The gate compares a per-run MINIMUM against a recorded MAXIMUM. That asymmetry is the machine's whole observed range given away for free, which is why the tolerance does not have to be large to absorb it — and why it has to be at least one more spread-width anyway, to cover the risk that the head lands on a machine worse than any yet seen. Twice the spread was the rule before the module split, when the observed spreads were 7-15%; applied to these it gives 0.80 and 0.98, and the schema's own validator refuses a tolerance at or above 1.0 precisely because a gate that cannot fail is not a gate. The rule that survives these numbers is therefore: TOLERANCE = THE OBSERVED SPREAD OF THAT POPULATION, taking the widest entry when several share one tolerance. That gives 0.40 for the unit suite (39.8%) and 0.50 for the renderer workloads (49.0%, rounded up). The rule travels; the number is derived from whichever cell reads it.

WHAT 0.40 AND 0.50 ACTUALLY BUY, STATED RATHER THAN LEFT TO BE ASSUMED. The ceilings are 32.4 CPU seconds for the suite and 0.126 / 1.79 / 0.106 for the three workloads. A DOUBLED workload is caught on three of the four entries even when measured on the fastest machine observed — the suite at 33.19 against a 32.4 ceiling, bench.render-impact at 2.038 against 1.79, bench.render-responsiveness at 0.1205 against 0.1064 — and is MISSED on bench.render, where doubling the fastest machine observed gives 0.113 against a 0.126 ceiling. Read plainly: this gate catches a near-doubling of the suite, of the workload that matters most, and of bench.render-responsiveness; it does not reliably catch a doubling of bench.render, the briefest workload, and it will not catch a 20% regression anywhere. That is the price of a counter this noisy on a pool this wide, and it is a limitation to state rather than a budget to tune until the limitation disappears.

WHY THE TWO POPULATIONS ARE SEPARATE RECORDS, WITH THREE DATA POINTS ACROSS THREE SCALES. The same machine effect, measured at three different scales, is the whole argument. bench.render spends 0.06-0.08 CPU seconds and spreads 49.0%: the fixed per-VM overhead IS the measurement. bench.render-impact spends 1.02-1.35 and spreads 32.6%. The unit suite spends 16.6-23.2 and spreads 39.8% in CPU but only 15.1% in WALL — a long run amortises the overhead further, and the wall figure says so before the CPU figure does. One wall or counter figure for all of them would have to be either too tight for the brief workloads, firing on ordinary pool variation, or so loose for the suite that it could not catch a suite that started waiting on something.

WHAT CHANGED SINCE THE PREVIOUS BASELINE, AND WHY THE PREVIOUS ONE WAS DELETED RATHER THAN CARRIED. The last committed baseline came from six dispatches at d051020, against a ghwidgets_common.py that the module split (ecd77b5) took apart into ghwidgets_cache.py, ghwidgets_journal.py and impact_clone.py, with d884584 moving impact clone and scratch ownership into a sibling. A split changes what the renderers import and therefore what they cost, so those envelopes were a measurement of a DIFFERENT PROGRAM and shipping them would have compared this tree against numbers that do not describe it. The file was deleted for that reason rather than left stale. Two directions of movement are visible across the split, and both are the code changing rather than the machine: the suite got MORE expensive and more stable (10.29-16.34 before, 16.59-23.20 now, with its wall spread tightening to 15.1%), because the split and main's eight commits made it longer and a longer run amortises the overhead further; and the renderer workloads got CHEAPER and tighter (bench.render-impact 0.771-1.415 before, 1.019-1.351 now, spread 83.6% down to 32.6%). Neither direction is a verdict about the split — it is what a counter's first measurement of a changed program looks like.

THE SMOKE BOUND. `wall` is recorded per entry as an envelope, for the same reason `entries` is: the spreads are 15.1-49.3%, so a single stored wall figure would be an arbitrary pick among min, median and max, and the gate compares against the recorded maximum so that SMOKE_FACTOR is a multiple of the worst wall actually observed. At SMOKE_FACTOR 3.0 the ceilings are 166.4 seconds, 0.255, 4.46 and 0.240 — comfortably above every spread above, which is what a cliff detector should be. The report prints no elapsed time at all: a verdict and no number.

HOW TO RE-DERIVE. Run the job at least four times on the cell that will read it — two is thin and one is refused — and take each entry's min and max across those dispatches, with n counting them. Re-derive, never carry: an envelope recorded on one machine and applied to another is the mistake this schema exists to make impossible, and the ratchet refuses any raise to a recorded maximum, so an improvement lowers the ceiling rather than being edited in.
